title: AI Chip Shipments Will Jump an Order of Magnitude: From a Million to 15 Million
dek: Broadcom's president shows an AI chip roadmap: from a million units to 15 million, with the 'beast' being the largest package of 8 stackable compute dies plus 16 HBM modules, and four of the five frontier labs are collaborating.
why: Broadcom rarely discloses details, but this time it gave three tiers of packaging and three tiers of shipment volumes, plus a clear judgment on the HBM bottleneck. For those tracking ASICs and packaging, these 11 minutes are more informative than many long analytical articles.
who: Investors and chip engineers focused on ASIC custom chips, advanced packaging, and the HBM supply chain, as well as founders who want to understand the custom chip strategies of OpenAI/Anthropic.
skip: Those familiar with back-end design services can skip 0:01–2:07; the key numbers come after 5:09.

points.h: Custom chip makers still outsource the final step
points.body: Google, Meta, Amazon, and some frontier model companies can have their own chip design teams, define their own architecture and interconnect, but ultimately they still have to 'get the thing built': dealing with foundries and development kits, managing the timing and latency of connections between transistors. Broadcom is the largest of these fee-based back-end design service providers. Clients come to it not just for design capability, but also for a batch of ready-made IP including high-speed I/O, high-speed compute, and memory controllers.

points.h: The most tight-lipped chip company suddenly starts talking
points.body: Broadcom is a mystery externally: it has almost no PR department and rarely discloses proactively. Occasionally it releases a Tomahawk network chip, or chats with Patrick Kennedy on ServeTheHome. Over the past year, president Charlie has rarely stood on stage to talk about what Broadcom is doing and why it is expanding its customer base from traditional network chips to AI custom chips. This chart showing three tiers of chips is the clue.

points.h: Today's AI servers are just the smallest of three tiers
points.body: Of the three tiers Charlie showed, the leftmost tier is already shipping in hundreds of thousands of systems, about the size of this Cisco chip on the table: one compute die in the middle, surrounded by four to six HBM modules, packaged similarly to TSMC's CoWoS. Broadcom says that over the past year, it has shipped more than one million units of this type of chip for customers. This tier is the reality of today's AI servers.

points.h: The larger the package, the higher the shipment volume
points.body: The middle tier is noticeably larger: two to four compute/IO dies, surrounded by eight to twelve HBM modules; AMD's MI455X also fits this design form. Charlie's expected shipment volumes are the key: the middle tier is expected to ship 5 million units, and the rightmost tier 15 million units. Placed next to 'one million units over the past year,' this is not linear growth but an order-of-magnitude jump in shipments for the next generation of AI custom chips.

points.h: The rightmost chip may stack compute dies on compute dies
points.body: The rightmost beast: the red parts are eight compute dies arranged in two columns of four rows, and they are stacked. Charlie lifts the red to reveal purple underneath; underneath could be SRAM, or SRAM could be on top; if it is compute-on-compute, it effectively equals sixteen compute dies. Each compute die is paired with two HBM modules, so one package contains sixteen HBM modules, with two light-blue IO dies at the top and bottom edges, and openings left at the package edges for optical modules.

points.h: Almost all frontier model companies are making their own chips
points.body: Charlie said that of the five most advanced frontier model labs, four are working with Broadcom on custom compute chips. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic define the designs they want, Broadcom does the back-end services and interfaces with TSMC, and then partners like Supermicro and WiWynn are brought in for data center scale deployment. This also explains why Broadcom is expanding capacity: it not only serves traditional network customers but is also taking orders from large model companies.

points.h: The bottleneck to scaling may not be packaging but HBM
points.body: The real bottleneck may not be packaging but whether there is enough high-bandwidth memory to go around: will there be new forms between DDR/LPDDR and HBM to fill the gap? Additionally, Broadcom said on stage that it has already deployed a 2nm chip with a partner, slightly smaller than the beast, and sooner. This reminds us that in the coming years, advanced packaging and HBM capacity will be swept up along with custom chip orders.

points.h: The first 2nm custom chip to land may come from Japan
points.body: The host pinned down the 'coming soon, smaller' 2nm chip Broadcom mentioned: he asked George from Chips and Cheese, and the two judged it to be Fujitsu's Monaka—a 2nm compute die paired with a 5nm SRAM die, with a central IO die in the middle. This chip has previously appeared at several conferences as a mockup or test silicon.

terms.def: The physical design phase after front-end chip design and before foundry production, including place and route, timing closure, etc.
High-bandwidth memory: DRAM stacked close to the compute chip via advanced packaging, with bandwidth far exceeding ordinary DDR/LPDDR.
TSMC's 2.5D packaging process that places multiple compute dies and HBM modules side by side on a silicon interposer.
A proprietary interconnect that connects multiple accelerator chips into one logical large machine, distinct from ordinary data center networking.
